repaired_payload.caption:
A sealed box isn't a guarantee of authenticity anymore. A recent discovery of a fake Ryzen 9 9950X3D2 processor—built on an Intel substrate—shows how sophisticated hardware scams have become. 

• Why factory seals are no longer foolproof
• The danger of buying from unverified sources
• How to spot a mismatch before you pay

Save this to protect your next tech purchase. If you bought a high-end component online, would you know how to verify the internal hardware before opening the box? 

#TechSecurity #HardwareScam #Ryzen9 #ConsumerSafety #MarketDebunk

slides.title: The Hidden Tax on 'Too-Good-To-Be-True' Deals
slides.body: A sealed box for a high-end Ryzen 9 9950X3D2 was opened, only to reveal an Intel substrate inside. Even factory-sealed products are now being compromised.

comparison_data.myth: A sealed box means the product inside is genuine and untouched.
comparison_data.reality: Packaging can be replicated or resealed, allowing fake or mismatched parts to pass as new.

stat_data.label: Incident Date
stat_data.context: The scam involving the Ryzen 9 9950X3D2 was officially documented on October 17, 2026, highlighting the 10th month of the year as a period of increased hardware fraud.

slides.title: How the Scam Works
slides.card_text: Scammers replace the internal processor with a cheaper or mismatched substrate (the base of the chip). They then reseal the box so perfectly that it looks like it came straight from the factory floor.

slides.title: Why This Matters for You
slides.card_text: When you buy expensive hardware, you aren't just paying for the box; you are paying for the performance inside. A mismatch means the device will either not work at all or fail to perform as promised.

slides.title: The Verification Process
flowchart_data: 1. Inspect the physical substrate markings for inconsistencies.
2. Check the serial number on the chip itself.
3. Cross-reference the serial number with the official manufacturer database.
